title: Evolution of knowledge – The hydrogen atom
header: Evolution of knowledge – The hydrogen atom

text.text:
### Prerequisites

This text explores the ideas we met in the previous text (<htcite0>) and uses them to explain how the atom itself is built. If fractions are still unfamiliar, we recommend studying that text before continuing.

### Introduction

When we first studied the atom (<htcite0>), we saw how our understanding of it has changed over time. In general terms, we could say that each generation has looked for something indivisible — a piece that could not be split any further.

As knowledge advanced, we left that idea behind and began to understand the atom as a structure built from smaller, elementary particles. In this text we take one more step along that path: we study the smallest atom we know, hydrogen, and see what it is made of.

Reflection 1: I Only Know That I Know Nothing

When we have little knowledge, we may believe we hold an unquestionable truth. However, as we deepen our studies, we realize there is always more to learn.

Have you ever had a certainty that you later abandoned after studying the subject more deeply?

### Atomic Models

The first explanation of the atom we studied — the Rutherford model — proposed an atom with a solid nucleus made of positive charges, the protons, and electrons moving around that nucleus. In the same study we also learned that, years later, another particle was found in the nuclei of heavy atoms: the neutron (<htcite0>).

#### Almost There

The Rutherford model explained some of the measurements observed in the atom, but not all of them. In other words, it still needed improvement. What exactly did it fail to explain?

#### Hydrogen

To understand what was missing, we will study the smallest atom we know — hydrogen. It is the simplest atom in nature, so it is also the best test for any atomic model: if a model cannot explain hydrogen, it will not explain larger atoms either.

Studies of the hydrogen atom show that its internal structure is simple (<htcite1>):
- a single proton in the nucleus;
- one electron orbiting that nucleus.

Using what we already know about fractions (<htcite2>), we can represent a hydrogen atom as:

1=22=1 + 12=12+12

Calculation 1: Representation of the hydrogen atom with two components (proton and electron).

**Calculation 1** shows how we can represent the atom with fractions. Read it like this: one hydrogen atom has two components (2/2) — two equal parts that together make the whole. One part is the electron orbiting the nucleus (1/2), and the other is the proton inside the nucleus (1/2).

Using the Rutherford model, we could draw it like this:
Chart 1: Representation of hydrogen according to the Rutherford model.
text.imgdesc: Representation of the atom according to the Rutherford model, in which there is a large positive nucleus and small electrons around it with negative charge.

text.text:
In **Chart 1** we see that the proton — the larger white circle with a plus sign (+) — is much larger than the electron — the smaller pink circle with a minus sign (–).

With this in mind, we can now look at what the Rutherford model could not explain.

#### The Bohr Atom

Light carries information about the matter that produced it. By spreading starlight into a spectrum and reading which colors are present, we can tell exactly what a star is made of (<htcite0>).

We can do the same in the laboratory. If continuous light passes through a gas and we spread out the light that comes through, some colors are missing: the gas absorbed them. Because each gas always absorbs the same set of colors, those missing lines act as a fingerprint that identifies the element (<htcite1>).

**Chart 2** shows this fingerprint for hydrogen — a simplified version of its spectrum, mapped by Lyman, Balmer, and Paschen (<htcite2>):

source.text: Merrill, P. W., & Wilson, O. C.

text.text: Chart 2: Spectrum of the hydrogen atom.
text.imgdesc: The spectrum is made up of vertical lines spaced according to the measurements taken.

text.text:
**Chart 2** shows that the spectrum is not a continuous band of colors: it is a series of separate lines with dark gaps in between. This observation is what led Bohr to refine the model proposed by Rutherford.

According to Bohr, electrons cannot move freely anywhere around the nucleus; they can only occupy well-defined orbits.

An electron jumps to a larger orbit when it absorbs energy (light) and falls back to a smaller orbit when it emits light (<htcite0>). Each of those jumps corresponds to one of the lines seen in **Chart 2**.

**Chart 3** shows Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom. In this representation the nucleus is colored yellow so that it can be distinguished from the possible electron orbits.
Chart 3: Representation of hydrogen according to the Bohr model.

### Expanding Knowledge

Another way to look inside matter is to smash particles into each other and study what comes out (**Figure 1**). That is what particle accelerators, such as CERN's Large Hadron Collider, are built for: besides producing new discoveries, these collisions let us confirm theoretical predictions — among them, the fact that protons and neutrons are themselves made of smaller particles (<htcite0>; <htcite1>).

source.page: Recreating Big Bang matter on Earth

text.text: Figure 1: Particles produced during the collision of protons. © CERN. ().

Our knowledge of the proton has kept evolving since its discovery (<htcite0>). We now know that a proton is not a fundamental particle: it is built from three smaller particles called quarks, which — like electrons — show no internal structure of their own.

Quarks come in several types; the ones found inside protons are called *up* and *down*. A proton contains exactly two *up* quarks and one *down* quark (<htcite1>) — a detail we will use in the next section.

Reflection 2: Representation

We began our study of the hydrogen atom with two particles and split them into two equal halves (1/2): one half for the electron, one half for the proton. Added back together, they return the whole atom (1).

We then discovered that the proton itself contains three elementary particles, the quarks. So hydrogen involves at least four fundamental particles.

How could we represent all of these elementary particles with fractions?

### Representing

Once again we use a sheet of paper, now divided to stand for each fundamental particle, so that we can connect fractions with the act of dividing.

Let us represent **Calculation 1** as a sheet cut in two: the left half stands for the electron and the right half for the proton, exactly as we did in the previous text (<htcite0>).

electronproton

Table 1: Sheet divided to represent the electron and the proton.
Since the proton contains three internal particles called quarks, we can see that the right half of the sheet (the proton) must now be divided into three equal parts:

electronproton
quark up
quark up
quark down

Table 2: Sheet divided to represent the electron and the proton with their quarks visible.

Before going on with the quark calculations, one warning: the sheet is only a way of keeping track of the parts. On paper the two halves look equally large, and splitting the proton into three rows makes its pieces look small, but none of this says anything about real sizes. Real sizes are the ones drawn in the Bohr model of **Chart 3**.

Now we can represent the particles with fractions.

#### Quarks in the Proton

Let us start with the proton alone. Taking the proton as one whole (1) divided into its three quarks — for now ignoring that two of them are *up* and one is *down* — we can write:

1=33=1 + 1 + 13=13+13+13

Calculation 2: Representation of the proton with three quarks.

#### Quarks and Protons in the Atom

**Calculation 2** shows the inside of the proton, but we must remember that in the whole atom this proton is only one half (1/2). Once again we use an idea from the previous text (<htcite0>): a fraction keeps its value when we multiply its numerator and its denominator by the same number.

So instead of treating the proton as the whole (1), we treat it as half of the atom (1/2) and multiply numerator and denominator by 3/3. Note that 3/3 is just 1, so the value does not change — the two halves are simply cut into three pieces each, giving sixths:

33(12)=3 × 13 × 2=36=16+16+16

Calculation 3: Division of the half into three parts.

### Reassembling the Whole

We have now separated the atom into its parts; the next step is to put them back together into a single atom.

Unlike in the previous texts, where we added pieces that had all been divided the same way, this time the two pieces are cut differently: half of the sheet stands for the electron (1/2), and the other half stands for the three quarks inside the proton (3/6).

Adding fractions that have different denominators therefore takes one extra step compared with simply adding the numerators (<htcite0>).

Reflection 3: What now?

The goal is to add the two parts (1/2 and 3/6) and get back the single atom (1).

How can two fractions with different denominators be added to give the whole?

As we have studied, the denominator of a fraction — the number at the bottom — tells us into how many equal parts the whole has been cut (<htcite0>). Two fractions can only be added once they are cut into the same number of parts.

Combining this with the idea that multiplication is the repeated addition of equal elements (<htcite1>), we can turn our two “different” fractions into comparable ones and add them to recover the whole.

#### Step by Step

The first step is to write down exactly what we want to add.

In our example, we add the elements of the electrosphere — the region where the electrons are found — to the elements of the nucleus, and the result must be the hydrogen atom:

The atom=electrosphere+nucleus

Calculation 4: Representation of the sum of the electrosphere and the nucleus.

In **Calculation 1** the atom is the whole (1). The electrosphere was defined as half of the atom (1/2), and the nucleus of the hydrogen atom — the other half — was identified as a single proton with three quarks (3/6).

1=12+36

Calculation 5: Representation of the elements of the hydrogen atom.

In the next step we must remember that in any process involving matter, matter is conserved (<htcite0>; <htcite1>). In an equation this has a practical meaning: whatever we do on the right-hand side, we must also do on the left-hand side, or the two sides stop being equal.

So first we rebuild the whole. Recall that the original total had two parts (2/2), while the quark discovery (3/6) comes in the next stage. Multiplying **Calculation 5** by 2 gives those two parts back:
2 × 1=2 × 12+2 × 36
2 × 1=22× 1+2 × 36

2=1+66

Calculation 6: Representation of the elements of the hydrogen atom.
**Calculation 6** still has a fraction on the right-hand side (6/6). Multiplying both sides by 6 clears it, because 6/6 × 6 = 6, and every term becomes a whole number while the two sides stay equal:
6 × 2=6 × 1+6 × 66
6 × 2=6 × 1+66×6
12=6+6

12=12

Calculation 7: Representation of the summed elements.
**Calculation 7** shows that the parts add up to a balanced equation: 12 = 12. To bring it back to a single atom, we divide both sides by 12 — the same as multiplying them by (1/12):
1212=1212

1=1

Calculation 8: Returning to the total.

Finally, we are back where we started: a single atom represented through fractions.

### Simplification Is Not Omission

In everyday life we often have so many tasks that we end up memorizing formulas and substituting numbers without ever understanding the whole.

For example, look at **Formula 1**, the rule for adding fractions, published by *Wolfram MathWorld* (<htcite0>):

ab+cd=(a × d) + (b × c)(b × d)

Formula 1: Sum of fractions.
Now, substituting the values:

12+36=(1 × 6) + (2 × 3)2 × 6=6 + 612=1212=1

Calculation 9: Sum of fractions using Formula 1.

Reflection 4: Same Result

If, by using a formula, we get the same result as when doing the process step by step, why do we need to go through the steps?

Formulas summarize what we understand about a phenomenon.

If the phenomenon itself is not understood, however, a formula is nothing more than a group of letters and symbols without meaning.

Every step we took from **Calculation 1** through **Calculation 8** is already contained in **Calculation 9**.

The fact that both give the same result is therefore no coincidence: the formula is the shortcut, and the steps are the reason that shortcut works.

### Conclusion

In this text we looked more closely at the hydrogen atom and saw how fractions let us represent the particles that compose an atom — the electron (1/2) and the proton with its three quarks (3/6) — and then rebuild the whole from those parts.

We also saw that everything we observe in nature can be summarized in a formula. But if we do not understand what we are studying, we will hardly be able to give a coherent explanation of the phenomenon: the steps are what give the formula its meaning.

exercise_v2.question: Does Rutherford's atomic model explain everything we know about the atom?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: Rutherford's model allowed electrons to orbit at any distance, so it cannot explain why atoms absorb and emit light only at specific wavelengths — the spectrum.

exercise_v2.question: Does Bohr's atomic model explain the spectrum of atoms?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: By allowing electrons only in specific orbits, gaining or releasing energy (light) as they jump between them, Bohr explained the spectrum that Rutherford's model could not.

exercise_v2.question: To add fractions with different denominators, must we combine all the parts?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: Adjusting the numerator and the denominator means cutting both fractions into the same number of equal parts, so that all the parts can then be grouped together.
